subject: chemistry

items.q:
Consider the four changes W, X, Y and Z below at 298 K. Which change results in an increase in the entropy of the system?
W: 2H₂S(g) + O₂(g) → 2S(s) + 2H₂O(l)   (exothermic)
X: NH₃(g) → NH₃(aq)   (exothermic)
Y: 2C(s) + O₂(g) → 2CO(g)   (exothermic)
Z: N₂(g) + 2O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g)   (endothermic)
items.correct: Change Y
items.misconception: Change W
items.why: Entropy is introduced as 'more particles, more disorder', and the rule 'more moles of product means an increase in entropy' is often stated without the words 'of gas'. Students then count coefficients across the whole equation, as they do for mole ratios. Look at the states first. Count only the moles of gas on each side: an increase in moles of gas gives a positive ΔS, a decrease gives a negative ΔS. Converting gas into solids or liquids lowers the entropy of the system even if more formula units are produced.
items.specStatementText: Entropy, S, is a measure of the dispersal or distribution of matter and/or energy in a system. The more ways the energy can be distributed, the higher the entropy. Under the same conditions, the entropy of a gas is greater than that of a liquid, which in turn is greater than that of a solid.

items.q:
Nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia:
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g)
Standard entropies: S⦵(N₂(g)) = 191.6 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, S⦵(H₂(g)) = 130.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, S⦵(NH₃(g)) = 192.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
What is the standard entropy change, ΔS⦵, for the reaction?
items.correct: −198.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: +385.6 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
items.why:
ΔH⦵f of an element in its standard state is zero by definition, and students carry this convention over from enthalpy cycles to entropy, not realizing that S⦵ values are absolute rather than values relative to the elements. Only enthalpies of formation are defined relative to the elements. Standard entropies of pure substances are measured from zero at absolute zero, so an element at 298 K has a positive S⦵ that must be included in ΣS⦵(products) − ΣS⦵(reactants).

Working: ΔS⦵ = ΣS⦵(products) − ΣS⦵(reactants) = 2(192.8) − [191.6 + 3(130.7)] = 385.6 − 583.7 = −198.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: Entropy, S, is a measure of the dispersal or distribution of matter and/or energy in a system. The more ways the energy can be distributed, the higher the entropy. Under the same conditions, the entropy of a gas is greater than that of a liquid, which in turn is greater than that of a solid.

items.q: For the Haber process reaction, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), ΔH⦵ = −92.2 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −198.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Assuming these values do not change with temperature, what is ΔG⦵ for the reaction at 450 °C?
items.correct: +51.0 kJ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: −3.1 kJ mol⁻¹
items.why:
Everyday and laboratory temperatures are stated in °C, and in many earlier calculations (such as Q = mcΔT) only a temperature change is used, which has the same size in °C and in K. Convert any Celsius temperature to kelvin before substituting it into ΔG⦵ = ΔH⦵ − TΔS⦵, T = ΔH⦵/ΔS⦵ or RT ln K. Only temperature differences are the same in both scales.

Working: T = 450 + 273 = 723 K. ΔS⦵ = −198.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = −0.1981 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. ΔG⦵ = ΔH⦵ − TΔS⦵ = −92.2 kJ mol⁻¹ − (723 K)(−0.1981 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) = −92.2 + 143.2 = +51.0 kJ mol⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: Change in Gibbs energy, ΔG, relates the energy that can be obtained from a chemical reaction to the change in enthalpy, ΔH, change in entropy, ΔS, and absolute temperature, T.

items.q: For the reaction 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g) at 150 °C, ΔG⦵ = −52.2 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −146.6 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH⦵ for the reaction?
items.correct: −114.2 kJ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: +9.8 kJ mol⁻¹
items.why:
Under time pressure, students rearrange by moving symbols rather than by adding the same quantity to both sides. Add TΔS⦵ to both sides: ΔH⦵ = ΔG⦵ + TΔS⦵. Check by substituting back.

Working: T = 150 + 273 = 423 K. ΔS⦵ = −146.6 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = −0.1466 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. ΔH⦵ = ΔG⦵ + TΔS⦵ = −52.2 kJ mol⁻¹ + (423 K)(−0.1466 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) = −52.2 − 62.0 = −114.2 kJ mol⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: Change in Gibbs energy, ΔG, relates the energy that can be obtained from a chemical reaction to the change in enthalpy, ΔH, change in entropy, ΔS, and absolute temperature, T.

items.q: For a reaction, ΔH⦵ is negative and ΔS⦵ is negative. Assuming that neither value changes with temperature, which statement about the reaction is correct?
items.correct: Spontaneous only when the temperature is low enough
items.misconception: Spontaneous only when the temperature is high enough
items.why: Raising the temperature increases the rate of almost every reaction, and heating is how reluctant reactions are made to 'go' in the laboratory, so students transfer this kinetic fact to feasibility. Separate rate from feasibility. Temperature affects feasibility only through the −TΔS term: it favours reactions with positive ΔS and disfavours those with negative ΔS. A faster rate at higher T does not change the sign of ΔG.
items.specStatementText: At constant pressure, a change is spontaneous if the change in Gibbs energy, ΔG, is negative.
items.random_wrong: Spontaneous at every temperature, however high or low

items.q:
Silicon is manufactured by heating silica with carbon:
SiO₂(s) + 2C(s) → Si(s) + 2CO(g)   ΔH⦵ = +690 kJ mol⁻¹
Standard entropies in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: SiO₂(s) 41.5, C(s) 5.7, Si(s) 18.8, CO(g) 197.7.
Assuming ΔH⦵ and ΔS⦵ do not change with temperature and ignoring any changes of state, above what temperature does the reaction become spontaneous?
items.why:
S⦵ values are read from a table one substance at a time, and students list them without returning to the equation to see how many moles of each substance react. ΔS⦵ refers to the molar amounts in the equation. For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), the sum for the reactants is S⦵(N₂) + 3 × S⦵(H₂) and for the products 2 × S⦵(NH₃).

Working: ΔS⦵ = ΣS⦵(products) − ΣS⦵(reactants) = [18.8 + 2(197.7)] − [41.5 + 2(5.7)] = 414.2 − 52.9 = +361.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. At the temperature where the reaction becomes spontaneous, ΔG⦵ = 0, so T = ΔH⦵/ΔS⦵ = (690 000 J mol⁻¹)/(361.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) = 1910 K (to the nearest kelvin). Above 1910 K, TΔS⦵ > ΔH⦵ and ΔG⦵ < 0.
items.specStatementText: At constant pressure, a change is spontaneous if the change in Gibbs energy, ΔG, is negative.
items.working: ΔS⦵ = ΣS⦵(products) − ΣS⦵(reactants) = [18.8 + 2(197.7)] − [41.5 + 2(5.7)] = 414.2 − 52.9 = +361.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. At the temperature where the reaction becomes spontaneous, ΔG⦵ = 0, so T = ΔH⦵/ΔS⦵ = (690 000 J mol⁻¹)/(361.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) = 1910 K (to the nearest kelvin). Above 1910 K, TΔS⦵ > ΔH⦵ and ΔG⦵ < 0.

items.q: For the change C(diamond) → C(graphite), ΔG⦵ = −2.9 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. Yet diamonds show no detectable conversion into graphite at room temperature, even over centuries. Which statement accounts for both facts?
items.correct: The change is spontaneous, but at 298 K its rate is negligible.
items.misconception: The change is not spontaneous, as it does not happen quickly.
items.why: In everyday English 'spontaneous' means sudden or immediate, and students are rarely shown feasible reactions that do not visibly occur. Thermodynamics (ΔG) tells whether a change can happen; kinetics (activation energy, rate) tells how fast. The conversion of diamond into graphite and the combustion of methane in air at room temperature are both spontaneous, yet neither occurs at a noticeable rate without intervention.
items.specStatementText: At constant pressure, a change is spontaneous if the change in Gibbs energy, ΔG, is negative.
items.random_wrong: The change needs a catalyst at 298 K to make its ΔG⦵ negative enough.

items.q: For the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g), ΔH⦵ = −197.8 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −188.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Which statement about the reaction at 298 K is correct?
items.correct: Spontaneous: the surroundings gain more entropy than the system loses.
items.misconception: Not spontaneous: the entropy of the system falls in this reaction.
items.why: The second law is often quoted as 'entropy always increases' without the words 'of the universe', so students apply it to the reacting chemicals alone and ignore the surroundings. Spontaneity is decided by ΔG, which includes both the entropy change of the system (ΔS) and that of the surroundings (through −ΔH/T). Water freezing below 0 °C and the formation of ammonia at 298 K both have negative ΔS for the system but are spontaneous.
items.specStatementText: At constant pressure, a change is spontaneous if the change in Gibbs energy, ΔG, is negative.
items.random_wrong: Spontaneous: an exothermic reaction is spontaneous whatever its ΔS⦵.

items.q: For a reaction at 25 °C, the equilibrium constant, K, is 5.00 × 10¹⁸. What is ΔG⦵ for the reaction at this temperature? (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
items.correct: −106.6 kJ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: −46.3 kJ mol⁻¹
items.why:
pH, pKa and pKw all use log₁₀, and the log₁₀ key is the one students use most, so they press 'log' (and '10ˣ') where 'ln' (and 'eˣ') is required. Use ln and eˣ in ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K and ΔG = ΔG⦵ + RT ln Q. ln x = 2.303 log₁₀ x, so using log₁₀ in place of ln is out by a factor of 2.303 in the exponent.

Working: T = 25 + 273 = 298 K. ln K = ln(5.00 × 10¹⁸) = 43.06. ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K = −(8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)(298 K)(43.06) = −1.066 × 10⁵ J mol⁻¹ = −106.6 kJ mol⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: As a reaction approaches equilibrium, ΔG becomes less negative and finally reaches zero.

items.q: A reaction mixture reaches equilibrium at constant temperature and pressure. Which statement about the equilibrium mixture is correct?
items.correct: ΔG for the reaction in this mixture has become zero.
items.misconception: ΔG⦵ for the reaction has become equal to zero.
items.why: ΔG and ΔG⦵ differ only by a small symbol, and the statement 'ΔG = 0 at equilibrium' is learned without the distinction between the actual mixture and the standard states. ΔG⦵ refers to all substances in their standard states and does not change as the reaction proceeds; ΔG = ΔG⦵ + RT ln Q changes with composition. At equilibrium Q = K and ΔG = 0, which gives ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K.
items.specStatementText: As a reaction approaches equilibrium, ΔG becomes less negative and finally reaches zero.
items.random_wrong: ΔG for the mixture has reached its most negative value.

items.q: For the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) at 450 °C, ΔG⦵ = −61.9 kJ mol⁻¹. In a particular mixture of the three gases at this temperature, [SO₂] = 0.500 mol dm⁻³, [O₂] = 0.250 mol dm⁻³ and [SO₃] = 0.00250 mol dm⁻³. What is ΔG for the reaction in this mixture? (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
items.correct: −117.2 kJ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: −55398.8 kJ mol⁻¹
items.why:
Enthalpy data are given in kJ mol⁻¹ and entropy data in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, and the equation itself carries no conversion factor, so students substitute the numbers without checking that the units match. R is given in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ while ΔG⦵ is quoted in kJ mol⁻¹, so the same mismatch arises in RT ln K and RT ln Q. Before substituting, write every quantity with its unit and convert ΔS⦵ to kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (for example −198.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = −0.1981 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). The same care is needed in T = ΔH⦵/ΔS⦵, and in ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K and ΔG = ΔG⦵ + RT ln Q, where R is in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and RT ln K or RT ln Q must be divided by 1000 to give kJ mol⁻¹.

Working: T = 450 + 273 = 723 K. Q = [SO₃]²/([SO₂]²[O₂]) = (0.00250)²/((0.500)²(0.250)) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴. RT = (8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)(723 K) = 6008 J mol⁻¹ = 6.008 kJ mol⁻¹. ln Q = ln(1.0 × 10⁻⁴) = −9.210. ΔG = ΔG⦵ + RT ln Q = −61.9 + 6.008(−9.210) = −61.9 − 55.3 = −117.2 kJ mol⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: As a reaction approaches equilibrium, ΔG becomes less negative and finally reaches zero.

items.q: For the decomposition of ammonia, 2NH₃(g) ⇌ N₂(g) + 3H₂(g), ΔG⦵ = +32.9 kJ mol⁻¹ at 25 °C. What is the value of the equilibrium constant, K, for this reaction at 25 °C? (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
items.why:
When rearranging to K = e^(−ΔG⦵/RT) students often drop the minus sign, and 'negative' is associated with 'less', so a negative ΔG⦵ is read as 'less product'. Keep the minus sign: K = e^(−ΔG⦵/RT). A negative ΔG⦵ gives an exponent that is positive and K > 1; a positive ΔG⦵ gives K < 1. Check with the sign rule: spontaneous in the forward direction under standard conditions means products are favoured.

Working: T = 25 + 273 = 298 K. ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K, so ln K = −ΔG⦵/RT = −(32 900 J mol⁻¹)/((8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)(298 K)) = −13.29. K = e^−13.29 = 1.7 × 10⁻⁶.
items.specStatementText: As a reaction approaches equilibrium, ΔG becomes less negative and finally reaches zero.

items.q: Does dissolving always increase the entropy of the system?
items.correct: No. Dissolving an ionic solid usually increases entropy, but dissolving a gas decreases it: the gas particles move from the gas phase into a liquid, where they are confined among solvent molecules.
items.misconception: Dissolving always increases entropy, because the substance spreads out through the solvent.
items.why: Dissolving an ionic solid such as sodium chloride, in which an ordered lattice breaks up and the ions spread through the water, is the standard textbook example of an entropy increase, and students generalize it to everything that dissolves. Compare the state before and after. A solid dissolving gains freedom, so its entropy usually increases. A gas dissolving loses the very high entropy of the gas phase, so the entropy of the system decreases, for example NH₃(g) → NH₃(aq).
items.specStatementText: Entropy, S, is a measure of the dispersal or distribution of matter and/or energy in a system. The more ways the energy can be distributed, the higher the entropy. Under the same conditions, the entropy of a gas is greater than that of a liquid, which in turn is greater than that of a solid.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a change that absorbs heat necessarily increase the entropy of the system?
items.correct: No. The sign of ΔS for the system depends on how the matter and energy of the chemicals are distributed after the change (chiefly the change in moles of gas and in state), not on whether heat is absorbed or released.
items.misconception: Entropy is a measure of the heat a system contains, so a change that absorbs heat increases the entropy of the system and one that releases heat decreases it.
items.why: Entropy has units containing joules and is described in terms of energy being 'dispersed', and students have spent years classifying reactions as exothermic or endothermic, so they read ΔS as another measure of heat transferred, conflating it with ΔH. ΔS of the system and ΔH are separate quantities. An endothermic reaction such as N₂(g) + 2O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g) still has a negative ΔS, because 3 mol of gas become 2 mol. The heat a reaction exchanges changes the entropy of the surroundings (ΔS(surroundings) = −ΔH/T), which is taken into account through the ΔH term in ΔG.

items.q: Is ΔS⦵ calculated as ΣS⦵(reactants) − ΣS⦵(products)?
items.correct: No. ΔS⦵ = ΣS⦵(products) − ΣS⦵(reactants): the change is always final state minus initial state.
items.misconception: ΔS⦵ is found by subtracting the entropies of the products from those of the reactants.
items.why: In bond enthalpy calculations students use 'bonds broken (reactants) minus bonds formed (products)', and they carry this reactants-first template over to entropy, which reverses the sign. Any change ΔX is final minus initial. ΔS⦵ = ΣS⦵(products) − ΣS⦵(reactants). A quick check: a reaction that reduces the moles of gas must give a negative ΔS⦵.
items.specStatementText: Entropy, S, is a measure of the dispersal or distribution of matter and/or energy in a system. The more ways the energy can be distributed, the higher the entropy. Under the same conditions, the entropy of a gas is greater than that of a liquid, which in turn is greater than that of a solid.

items.q: Does the −TΔS⦵ term always make ΔG⦵ smaller than ΔH⦵?
items.correct: No. If ΔS⦵ is negative, −TΔS⦵ is positive and ΔG⦵ is greater (less negative) than ΔH⦵.
items.misconception: The −TΔS⦵ term is always subtracted as a positive amount, whatever the sign of ΔS⦵.
items.why: The equation contains a minus sign and ΔS⦵ is often negative, so students must handle 'minus a negative'; under time pressure one of the two signs is dropped and TΔS⦵ is simply taken away from ΔH⦵. Substitute ΔS⦵ with its sign in brackets: ΔG⦵ = ΔH⦵ − T(ΔS⦵). For ΔS⦵ = −0.1981 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ the term −T(−0.1981) is positive, so ΔG⦵ is less negative than ΔH⦵.

items.q: Is every exothermic reaction spontaneous?
items.correct: No. Spontaneity depends on the sign of ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. An exothermic reaction with a negative ΔS becomes non-spontaneous above the temperature at which TΔS outweighs ΔH.
items.misconception: A reaction that releases heat is spontaneous whatever its entropy change, so the sign of ΔH alone decides whether a reaction is spontaneous.
items.why: Most familiar reactions, such as combustion and neutralization, are exothermic and happen readily, and earlier courses present the release of energy as the reason reactions 'go'. A negative ΔH favours spontaneity but does not guarantee it. When ΔS is negative, −TΔS is positive and grows with temperature; above T = ΔH/ΔS the reaction is no longer spontaneous. The Haber process reaction is exothermic but has ΔG⦵ > 0 at high temperatures.
items.specStatementText: At constant pressure, a change is spontaneous if the change in Gibbs energy, ΔG, is negative.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a catalyst make ΔG more negative?
items.correct: No. A catalyst provides a pathway with a lower activation energy; it changes the rate but not ΔH, ΔS, ΔG⦵ or K.
items.misconception: A catalyst makes a reaction more thermodynamically favourable, making ΔG more negative so that a reluctant reaction can occur.
items.why: A catalyst 'makes a reaction go' in practice, so students attribute to it an effect on whether the reaction is favourable, not only on how fast it proceeds. ΔG depends only on the initial and final states, not on the route between them. A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so it changes the rate at which a spontaneous reaction proceeds but cannot make a non-spontaneous reaction spontaneous.
items.specStatementText: At constant pressure, a change is spontaneous if the change in Gibbs energy, ΔG, is negative.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does ΔG become more and more negative as a reaction approaches equilibrium?
items.correct: No. As a spontaneous reaction proceeds towards equilibrium, ΔG becomes less negative and finally reaches zero.
items.misconception: ΔG becomes steadily more negative as a reaction proceeds and is at its most negative when equilibrium is reached.
items.why: The Gibbs energy of the mixture, G, does fall to a minimum at equilibrium, and students confuse G itself with ΔG. A negative ΔG is also learned as 'favourable', which suggests that the further a reaction goes, the more negative ΔG should become. ΔG is the change in Gibbs energy per mole of reaction at the current composition, the driving force for further reaction. It is most negative at the start, when Q is far from K, becomes less negative as Q approaches K, and is zero at equilibrium, where G is at its minimum.
items.specStatementText: As a reaction approaches equilibrium, ΔG becomes less negative and finally reaches zero.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Have the forward and reverse reactions stopped once equilibrium is reached?
items.correct: No. At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so the composition no longer changes (dynamic equilibrium).
items.misconception: At equilibrium the reaction has stopped, because the reactants and products no longer change in amount.
items.why: The constant composition is what students observe, and everyday 'equilibrium' (a balanced, still object) suggests that nothing is happening. Equilibrium is dynamic: both reactions continue at equal rates. ΔG = 0 means there is no net driving force in either direction, not that the particles have stopped reacting.
items.specStatementText: As a reaction approaches equilibrium, ΔG becomes less negative and finally reaches zero.

items.q: Can Q be written with the reactants on top?
items.correct: No. Q has the same form as the equilibrium expression for the reaction as written: products (raised to their coefficients) over reactants (raised to their coefficients).
items.misconception: Q can be written either way up, or taken as the expression for the reverse reaction, without changing ΔG.
items.why: Students who have met the reverse reaction or are unsure which way round the expression goes invert it, and the effect of inverting Q (changing the sign of ln Q) is not obvious from the size of the numbers. Write Q for the equation as given: for N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), Q = [NO₂]²/[N₂O₄]. Inverting it changes the sign of RT ln Q and can reverse the predicted direction of reaction.
